claims.text: A longitudinal case study of a real-world consumer app using agentic infrastructure to personalise marketing messaging over 11 months compared an active phase (marketers curated content, audiences and strategies) with a passive phase (agents operated autonomously from a fixed library of components).

In the marketing personalisation case study, agents assembled messages by selecting atomic content components (e.g. value propositions, greetings, visual assets) via a sequential decision-making framework.

During the active human-managed phase of the marketing personalisation study, days with direct app opens attributable to push notifications rose +65.3% (±1.31), days with positive engagement +2.8% (±0.19), days with intent +0.3% (±0.23), and days with conversions +0.3% (±0.24).

After manual content injection and optimisation stopped for 7 months, autonomous marketing agents sustained a +57% (±0.11) lift in notification clicks, +2.4% (±0.21) days with engagement per user, and +0.2% (±0.27) lift in intent and conversion metrics, not reverting to baseline.

Moving to fully autonomous operation dampened lift by roughly 15% for overall engagement, 12% for notification opens, and 26% for days with intent and days with conversion events per user, relative to the active phase.

EnDevSols built a LangGraph multi-agent content system with a Supervisor Agent orchestrating sub-agents for research, SEO drafting and multi-lingual localization, on a FastAPI backend with a custom UI triggered by CSV uploads or prompts.
The EnDevSols content system uses a human-in-the-loop pending queue so every AI-generated post is reviewed against brand standards before one-click publishing to WordPress.
In the EnDevSols system, an SEO Auditor agent cross-references drafts against real-time search data before the Translation agent sees the text, preserving content across 10+ languages.

EnDevSols reports (vendor case study) time-to-publish falling from 48–72 hours to under 15 minutes, 95% fewer manual content tasks, 10x monthly output without added headcount, and 30% better international SEO rankings in the first quarter.

The Autonomous Sales Fleet is a production agentic-sales system built on LangGraph StateGraphs (control plane), Cloudflare D1/Workers/Queues (data plane), and LangSmith tracing with per-graph golden datasets (observability plane).

In the Autonomous Sales Fleet, all LLM calls go through one DeepSeek endpoint behind a Cloudflare AI Gateway, no graph ships unless its golden dataset passes an eval gate, and every persisted AI decision carries a four-field provenance record.

The Autonomous Sales Fleet's lead-to-proposal pipeline uses three agents that qualify, research from grounded facts, and draft a proposal unattended, with a single human gate on the send; outreach is always draft-first and held for human approval.
The Autonomous Sales Fleet applies a ≥0.80 eval bar to every prompt path.
A cited study (Maiorano, 2026, arXiv:2603.15676) found human reviewers and an automated quality gate agreed at only kappa = 0.13 in a multi-agent conversational system, barely above chance.

Tavon built a production RFP sales automation for a parts supplier on the Pi agent framework and OpenClaw: a gateway monitors an email inbox, triages and routes messages to one dedicated agent per customer.

Each Tavon customer agent is configured by an agent config file (harness, role, instructions) and a customer-specific file (special discounts, access rights, requirements, communication preferences), and uses CLI tools to access CRM and ERP systems in sandboxed environments with per-case sessions.
Tavon's agents do not send emails automatically; they place draft responses in the user's email client for review, editing and approval before sending.
OpenClaw adds multi-channel routing, provider orchestration, sub-agent management and gateway support on top of the Pi framework's core agent and session mechanics.
The Tavon case reports no scale, accuracy or business outcome data, shows a single example, and leaves unclear how often drafts need human editing.

Oliv.ai describes a sales multi-agent system with three layers: a commoditised data layer capturing activity, a fine-tuned LLM intelligence layer extracting signals like MEDDICC, and specialist agents coordinated by an orchestrator producing follow-ups, reports and next steps.

Oliv.ai defines three maturity levels: Augmented (AI drafts, human does the work), Assisted (agents execute, humans approve before shipping), and Autonomous (agents run end to end, humans handle exceptions); it claims one operator runs about '1.2 humans plus 20 agents' doing the work of 10 GTMs.

IBM's reference architecture uses watsonx Orchestrate as the orchestration plane with MCP for tool integration, A2A for agent collaboration and watsonx.governance, including supervisor/sub-agent hierarchies and a HITL gate pattern with state persisted at the checkpoint.
IBM's guidance says human-escalation thresholds should be risk-calibrated, such as financial transactions above a limit, irreversible actions or low-confidence decisions.

LangGraph supports human approval gates for high-risk steps such as updating a system, sending a customer message or escalating an incident; a cited benchmark found it more than twice as fast as CrewAI over 100 runs of a five-agent workflow.

The Poochaman multi-agent-orchestration repository documents sales, research and execution agents with structured handoffs, bounded retries, human escalation, and a runnable Python example of approvals, tenant isolation and mock CRM recovery.
